intro:
This track asks two questions that every system with copies on several computers must answer. When you read from one copy, what may it return? And how can computers that crash and lose messages agree on anything at all? Lessons start from scenes everyone knows: a shared card whose balance jumps back for a moment, a payment alert that arrives before the payment shows in the app, six people booking the last seat on a flight, a payout that reaches the shops twice. Then they open up the machinery, in simulators you can break on purpose and in real systems on your laptop.

By the end, you can:

- read a short history of reads and writes and say which consistency promise it keeps, from linearizable, where the copies behave like one, down to eventual;
- tell serializable from linearizable, and say what CAP and PACELC really cost;
- explain why a shared log, a one-winner decision and consensus are one problem, and how Paxos stays safe through a crash;
- trace a Raft election, a commit and a leader crash, and say why a new leader never loses a saved entry;
- elect a leader through ZooKeeper or etcd, and fence a frozen one with a token so it can't write after it has lost;
- say how Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB and Aurora DSQL put their transactions in order, and what each one charges for it.

The six lessons:

1. Consistency models: what a read may return
2. Linearizability: one copy, one timeline
3. Total order broadcast and the many faces of consensus
4. Consensus with Raft
5. Coordination services: ZooKeeper, etcd and KRaft
6. Distributed SQL: Spanner, CockroachDB and Aurora DSQL

You need to read a little code, in Kotlin or Java. The track builds on four earlier ones: Replication (copies, leaders and followers), Partitioning (splitting data by key), Transactions (isolation levels, versions and two-phase commit) and Faults, time and truth (partial failure, clocks, pauses and fencing tokens). Each lesson reminds you of what it borrows, and every term is explained the first time it appears.

The labs are plain Kotlin on a pretend clock, so a minute of elections, leases or clock drift runs in milliseconds, and the same seed, a starting number for every random choice, always gives the same run. Several use property tests (jqwik) that throw hundreds of random seeds at your code. Lessons 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 live in `labs/sim` (packages `sfz.cons.l01` to `l06`), and lesson 4's Raft lab lives in `labs/internals`. Run one from `labs/` with `./gradlew :sim:test --tests 'sfz.cons.l05.*'` (or `:internals:test` for lesson 4); the finished answers are in `src/solution`. None of the labs needs Docker. A few Try its run real systems in Docker, a free program that runs small, separate Linux systems on your computer: a MongoDB replica set in lesson 1, ZooKeeper, etcd and a three-node Kafka cluster in lesson 5, and CockroachDB in lesson 6. Start one at a time, and remove it when the Try it ends.
cheatsheet:
## Consistency models: what a read may return

A consistency model is a promise about which values a read may return when the data has several copies.

| Model | The promise | Every copy keeps answering when the network splits? |
|---|---|---|
| Strict serializable | transactions as if one at a time, in the order they really happened (Spanner: external consistency) | no |
| Linearizable | one value behaves like one copy: each operation takes effect at one instant inside its call, and once anyone reads a new value, no later read returns an older one | no |
| Sequential | one order that keeps each client's own order, but not real time | no |
| Causal | a cause is always seen before its effect, everywhere | only if each client sticks to one copy |
| Session guarantees | read your own writes, never go back in time, writes in order, writes after the reads they depend on | only if each client sticks to one copy |
| Eventual | the copies end up the same once writes stop | yes |
| Serializable | transactions as if one at a time, in some order; reads may be stale | no |
| Snapshot isolation | each transaction reads one snapshot; two writes to the same row clash; write skew allowed | no |

Linearizable is about one value and how recent a read is; serializable is about transactions and their order. Neither implies the other.

CAP, as Gilbert and Lynch proved it: when messages can be lost, no system can be linearizable and keep every copy answering. PACELC: even with no fault, stronger promises cost waiting on every request (etcd: 0.7 ms for an up-to-date read against 0.3 ms for a local one). Stores let you choose per request: Cassandra's levels, DynamoDB's `ConsistentRead`, MongoDB's `readConcern` and `w`, PostgreSQL's `synchronous_commit`, Kafka's `acks`. Defaults usually sit below linearizable.

## Who gives linearizability

| Setup | Linearizable? |
|---|---|
| One leader, every read and write on the real leader | yes, if the leader knows it still leads |
| Consensus (Raft, Paxos) with checked reads (ReadIndex or a lease) | yes |
| A leader that reads without checking it still leads | no: a replaced leader serves old data |
| Several leaders, or majority reads and writes (w + r > n) | no: two reads can disagree about a write in progress; ABD's write-back fixes reads and writes, not compare-and-set |

Checking a history for linearizability is a search for an order; do it one key at a time. Tools: Knossos, Porcupine, and Lincheck for Java and Kotlin classes.

## Consensus

Consensus: servers that can crash and lose messages agree on one value. Its rules are agreement, integrity, validity (safety) and termination (progress). These are one problem in disguise: consensus, a linearizable compare-and-set, total order broadcast (one log, read in the same order everywhere) and atomic commit that survives a crash. FLP: when delays have no limit, no fixed method can promise to finish if one server may crash, so real methods are always safe and use timeouts to make progress.

| | Paxos | Raft |
|---|---|---|
| Numbered period | ballot | term |
| Choosing who leads | prepare and promise (a majority) | RequestVote (a majority), granted only to a log at least as up to date |
| Copying | accept (a majority); Multi-Paxos: one round trip per command | AppendEntries, checked with prevLogIndex and prevLogTerm |
| Committed when | a majority accepted it under one ballot | an entry of the current term is on a majority (Figure 8) |
| Safe reads | leader with a lease, or a check with a majority | ReadIndex (one heartbeat round), or a clock-based lease |
| Changing members | left to whoever builds it | joint consensus, or one server at a time after the leader commits its no-op |

2f + 1 servers survive f failures: 3 survive 1, 5 survive 2, and 4 still survive only 1. Raft draws random election timeouts (150 to 300 ms in the paper; etcd defaults to a 100 ms heartbeat and a 1,000 ms timeout) and needs broadcast time ≪ election timeout ≪ time between failures. Every vote and entry reaches the disk before the reply. More servers make writes slower (ZooKeeper: 21,000 writes a second on 3 servers, 8,000 on 13).

## Coordination services

| Tool | ZooKeeper 3.9 | etcd 3.7 | Kafka 4 (KRaft) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compare-and-set | `create` fails if the znode exists; versioned `setData` | `Txn` with comparisons | changes checked by the active controller |
| Change counter | zxid, cZxid, cversion | one cluster revision; create_revision, mod_revision | offset in `__cluster_metadata`, and epochs |
| Noticing a dead client | session; EPHEMERAL znodes vanish with it | lease with a TTL; attached keys vanish with it | broker heartbeats; quiet brokers are fenced |
| Being told of changes | one-shot watches (persistent ones since 3.6) | watches from any revision still kept | brokers read the metadata log |
| Reads | from the local copy; `sync` first for the latest | up to date by default, local on request | brokers apply the log |

Recipes: leader election and locks (lowest sequence number or create_revision wins; watch only the one right before yours), service discovery (keys under a lease plus a watch; slightly old reads are fine), work assignment (one key, compare-and-set on its revision). No lock gives one holder at a time on its own: fence every write with the leader key's revision, checked by the resource in the same step as the write. Jepsen measured about 18% lost updates with unfenced etcd locks and 2-second leases.

## Distributed SQL

Key ranges on many machines + a consensus group per range + two-phase commit with intents and a replicated transaction record + versioned rows read at commit timestamps.

| System | Timestamps from | A write pays | A read pays | Default isolation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| TiDB | an oracle (the Placement Driver) | oracle trips, two-phase commit over Raft | an oracle trip | snapshot (REPEATABLE READ), with locks |
| FoundationDB | a sequencer | a version, a resolver check (5-second limit) | a read version | strict serializable |
| Spanner | TrueTime [earliest, latest] | commit wait of about 2ε (ε about 1 to 7 ms in 2012), overlapped with Paxos | may wait on recent writes | serializable; REPEATABLE READ on request |
| CockroachDB | hybrid logical clock, max offset 500 ms | one consensus round (parallel commits) | a restart if a value falls in (T, T + max offset] | serializable; READ COMMITTED on request |
| Aurora DSQL | adjudicators at commit | one adjudication, one journal write | nothing extra | snapshot only; 3,000 rows, 10 MiB, 5 minutes |

Retry on SQLSTATE 40001 with an idempotency key, set the isolation level yourself, and watch how far the clocks drift.
recap: A consistency model is a promise about which values a read may return. From strictest to loosest: linearizable, sequential, causal, the session guarantees and eventual. Serializable and snapshot isolation are about transactions, and strict serializable is linearizable and serializable at once.

No model at or above sequential keeps every copy answering when the network splits (CAP), and even with no fault, stronger promises cost waiting on every request (PACELC). Stores let you choose per request, and their defaults are usually below linearizable.

Linearizability needs a leader that knows it still leads, or consensus with checked reads. Majority reads and writes (w + r > n) aren't enough. Checking a history means searching for an order, one key at a time.

Consensus, a linearizable compare-and-set, one shared log and crash-proof atomic commit are one problem. FLP says no method can promise to finish when delays have no limit, so real methods are always safe and use timeouts to make progress.

Paxos decides a value with two round trips to a majority. Multi-Paxos and Raft keep a stable leader and pay one round trip and one disk flush per write. 2f + 1 servers survive f failures, and more servers make writes slower.

Raft: terms with at most one leader, votes only for logs at least as up to date, a check on the entry before each new one, commit by counting only current-term entries, ReadIndex or leases for reads, and membership changes one server at a time after the new leader's no-op commits.

Coordination services (ZooKeeper, etcd, Kafka's KRaft controllers) keep a few slow-changing facts and offer four tools: compare-and-set, a change counter, sessions with ephemeral keys, and watches. Elections, discovery and locks are short recipes on top.
No lease or lock stops a frozen holder from acting late. Fence every write with a token from consensus, such as the leader key's revision, and let the resource refuse lower ones.

Distributed SQL stacks key ranges, a Raft or Paxos group per range, two-phase commit and versioned rows. Where the timestamps come from sets the promise and the price: an oracle's round trip, Spanner's commit wait, CockroachDB's restarts, or DSQL's optimistic snapshot isolation.

quiz.q: A banking app writes a new balance on the leader, the copy that takes writes. The user's next page is served by a follower, a copy that is 2 seconds behind, and it shows the old balance. Which promise is broken, and what is the cheapest fix?
options: Serializability; run every transaction at SERIALIZABLE
Read your writes; send that user's reads to the leader for a short while, or read at a position at least as new as their last write
Linearizability; replace the database with a consensus store
Eventual consistency; wait for the follower to catch up
quiz.why: The user saw their own write disappear, which breaks the read-your-writes session guarantee. It only covers one user's session, so tracking that session's last write position is enough; full linearizability would make every read pay for it. Serializability is about transactions, and allows exactly this kind of stale read, which rules out the first option.

quiz.q: Cassandra, a database that keeps several copies of each row, stores 3 copies, and every write and every read waits for 2 of them (QUORUM). So every read overlaps every write. Is it linearizable?
options: Yes: w + r > n guarantees it
Only if all clocks are synchronized
No: a read during a write can get the new value from one copy while a later read gets the old value from two others; reads must write back before returning (ABD), and compare-and-set needs consensus
Only for tables with one row
quiz.why: Overlap guarantees that a read sees the latest finished write, not that two reads agree about a write still in progress. Once one reader has seen the new value, a later reader can still meet two copies without it, which is why the first option fails. Writing the value back to a majority before returning closes that gap for reads and writes. A linearizable compare-and-set needs consensus, which is what Cassandra's lightweight transactions add.

quiz.q: Why can't any fixed consensus method promise to finish when delays have no limit and one server may crash (FLP), and how does Raft live with that?
options: Messages can be corrupted; Raft uses checksums
Majorities can't overlap; Raft uses two-thirds majorities
Clocks drift; Raft uses atomic clocks

A slow server can't be told from a dead one, so the method can be kept undecided forever; Raft never breaks its safety rules and uses random timeouts, so it decides whenever the network behaves for a while
quiz.why: FLP is about finishing, not safety: an unlucky schedule can always delay the one message that would let the method decide. Raft keeps its safety rules unconditional, and only its progress depends on timing, through election timeouts. Real networks behave well enough most of the time, which is the partial synchrony Raft relies on.

quiz.q: In single-decree Paxos, a proposer's prepare(5) gets promises from a majority, and one acceptor reports that it already accepted the value "void" under ballot 3. The proposer wanted "capture". What must it send?
options: accept(5, "void"): it must adopt the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal it heard about
accept(5, "capture"): its own value, since it holds the higher ballot
Nothing: it must start again with ballot 6
accept(3, "void")
quiz.why: "void" may already be chosen by a majority that the proposer didn't hear from in full. Any majority overlaps that one, so the proposer saw at least one acceptor with "void", and the rule to adopt the highest-numbered accepted value keeps a chosen value chosen. Proposing its own value, the second option, could choose a second value.

quiz.q: A new Raft leader for term 7 finds an entry from term 5 at index 40, stored on four of its five servers. When may it treat index 40 as committed?
options: At once: four of five is a majority
Only when all five store it
Once an entry from term 7 after it is stored on a majority; index 40 is committed along with it
Never: entries from old terms are thrown away
quiz.why: This is Raft's Figure 8. A leader counts copies only for entries of its own term, because an old-term entry on a majority can still be overwritten by a server elected with a newer last term. That's why the first option fails. Committing the leader's no-op, or any term-7 entry, on a majority commits every earlier entry, through the Log Matching Property.

quiz.q: A store built on Raft has a leader that answers reads from memory. A network fault cuts it off, and the other servers elect a new leader that commits a refund. A client then reads from the old leader. What should the old leader have done before answering?
options: Nothing; its log holds every committed entry
Confirm it still leads with a heartbeat round to a majority (ReadIndex), or rely on a lease that assumes clocks run at nearly the same rate and nothing freezes
Pass the read to a random follower
Write the read into its log and wait for its own commit
quiz.why: A leader holds every entry committed before its term began, not entries committed after it was replaced, so the first option fails. ReadIndex costs one round trip and no disk write; a lease costs none, but trusts clocks. Writing the read into the log would also work, but it costs as much as a write, and a cut-off leader could never commit it anyway.

quiz.q: A program registers each of its running copies in etcd under a lease, and its nightly payout job takes a lock in etcd the same way. Which statement is right?
options: Finding the running copies can use cached or local reads, since callers cope with dead copies anyway; the payout lock needs fencing, because a holder frozen past its lease can still write
Both need up-to-date reads and fencing
Neither needs fencing, because etcd uses Raft
Finding the running copies needs fencing, and the lock doesn't
quiz.why: A list of running copies can be a second old: a caller that reaches a dead copy fails and tries another. A lock that guards a payout is about correctness. Consensus inside etcd can't stop a frozen program from writing to the payout store after its lease ends, which rules out the third option. The leader key's revision, checked by the store, can.

quiz.q: A ZooKeeper client crashes without closing its session. Its ephemeral znode marks it as the leader. What happens next?
options: The znode disappears the moment the network connection drops
The znode stays until someone deletes it by hand
Another client can delete it at once, because it's ephemeral
The znode stays until the ensemble expires the session, after its timeout passes with no heartbeat; then it's deleted, and the next candidate's watch fires
quiz.why: The ensemble, not the client, decides when a session is dead, and only after the agreed timeout (2 to 20 times tickTime). Until then the crashed client still looks like the leader. So a takeover takes about one session timeout, and the timeout is a trade between fast takeover and false alarms when a program merely freezes. The first option is tempting, but ZooKeeper goes by the session, not the connection.

quiz.q: Spanner and CockroachDB both make a transaction's timestamp agree with real time, yet only one of them makes every write wait. Why?
options: CockroachDB doesn't copy writes to other servers

Spanner's clocks have a small, known error (TrueTime), so waiting it out on each commit is cheap; CockroachDB's bound on ordinary clocks is large (500 ms by default), so it makes readers that meet an uncertain value restart instead
Spanner uses an oracle
CockroachDB only runs in one region
quiz.why: Commit wait costs about twice the clock error on every write: a few milliseconds with TrueTime, but far too much with a 500 ms bound. CockroachDB moves the cost to reads of keys written very recently, which happen less often. Neither uses an oracle, which rules out the third option; TiDB does.

quiz.q: A hospital's rota app has a rule: at least one doctor stays on call. It relied on PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE level to keep the rule, and the team moves it to Aurora DSQL. What should they expect?
options: Exactly the same behaviour: DSQL is distributed SQL, so it's serializable
Deadlocks under load
Write skew: DSQL offers only snapshot isolation, which checks only clashing writes; they need a shared row that both transactions write, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which DSQL checks as a write
Lost updates on single rows
quiz.why: Two transactions that each read both doctors and take a different one off call don't clash under snapshot isolation, so both commit, and nobody is left on call. DSQL has no deadlocks, since nothing waits on locks, and it does catch two writes to the same row, which rules out the second and last options. Distributed SQL doesn't mean serializable: read the isolation level before you move.
